families.name: Procedural and Generative Synthesis
families.definition: Methods that synthesize new 3D articulated objects or enhance static models into interactive ones using generative models, procedural tools, or diffusion priors.

properties.text: These methods use hierarchical transformers, diffusion models, or procedural toolboxes to generate geometry and kinematic structures simultaneously.
They can convert static 3D objects into openable or articulated versions by detecting parts and predicting motion.
Generative approaches often parameterize objects as trees of tokens or graphs to model part connectivity and articulation.
Some methods leverage 2D diffusion priors to provide virtual supervision for 3D shape and articulation learning.
They aim to create large-scale datasets with rich annotations to overcome data scarcity in articulated object understanding.

limitations.text: Generated objects may lack physical plausibility or detailed interior geometry if not explicitly constrained.
Flexibility-quality tradeoffs exist, where high flexibility often leads to lower geometric quality.
Many methods rely on predefined structures or retrieve shapes from static datasets, limiting diversity.
Physical validity of generated samples is a challenge, particularly in few-shot settings.

families.name: Reconstruction from Visual Observations
families.definition: Techniques that recover 3D shape, part segmentation, and articulation parameters from 2D images, videos, or point clouds.

properties.text: These methods use implicit representations like Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) or Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) to model geometry and appearance.
They often employ analysis-by-synthesis frameworks to optimize for part-level motion and shape from monocular or multi-view inputs.
Some approaches use skeleton-based or part-based models to handle non-rigid deformations and articulations.
Methods can reconstruct articulated objects from sparse image ensembles, single videos, or even single images.
They frequently utilize differentiable rendering to align 3D predictions with 2D observations.

limitations.text: Reconstruction from monocular inputs is inherently under-constrained and prone to ambiguities in pose and shape.
Many methods rely on pre-built deformable models or templates, limiting generalization to novel categories.
Heavy occlusion and complex dynamics in human-object interactions make accurate reconstruction difficult.
Real-time performance is often sacrificed for high-fidelity reconstruction, or vice versa.

families.name: Articulation and Kinematics Estimation
families.definition: Algorithms that identify movable parts, infer joint types, and estimate kinematic parameters from static or dynamic data.

properties.text: These methods detect openable parts and predict their motion parameters, such as joint axes and limits.
They can infer kinematic hierarchies and part connectivity from point cloud sequences or interaction data.
Some approaches use screw theory or equivariant networks to model part mobility and transformations.
They often operate in a self-supervised or semi-supervised manner to reduce the need for labeled motion data.
Methods can estimate articulation models from pairs of static states or from video sequences of moving objects.

limitations.text: Estimating articulation for unseen object categories remains challenging due to geometric and semantic variations.
Many methods assume a fixed kinematic structure or category-level priors, which limits generalizability.
Noisy point clouds in real-world settings degrade the performance of models trained on clean simulation data.
Inferring complete kinematic hierarchies for novel instances without templates is an open challenge.

families.name: Robot Manipulation and Interaction
families.definition: Systems that enable robots to perceive, plan, and execute actions to manipulate articulated objects in physical or simulated environments.

properties.text: These methods learn manipulation policies that generalize across different object categories and articulation structures.
They often use affordance prediction to identify actionable points on objects for pushing, pulling, or opening.
Some systems use imitation learning from human demonstrations or self-guided exploration to learn manipulation skills.
They integrate perception of object state with motion planning to execute complex tasks like opening cabinets or doors.
Benchmarks and simulators provide environments for training and evaluating these manipulation policies.

limitations.text: Generalization to novel object categories and unseen instances is a significant hurdle.
Sim-to-real transfer is difficult due to differences in physics, sensing, and actuation.
Many methods require extensive interaction data or human demonstrations, which are costly to collect.
Handling dynamic obstacles and complex scene interactions in real-world environments remains challenging.

families.name: Human-Object Interaction (HOI) Modeling
families.definition: Approaches that model the interaction between humans and articulated objects, including pose estimation, motion synthesis, and dataset creation.

properties.text: These methods capture full-body human motion and object articulation during interactions, such as grasping or opening.
They often use motion capture data or video-based reconstruction to create datasets of human-object interactions.
Some approaches synthesize human motions conditioned on textual instructions or object states.
They aim to understand the spatial arrangements and contact points between humans and objects.
Methods can reconstruct 3D human and object poses from monocular videos or single images.

limitations.text: Heavy occlusion between humans and objects makes accurate 3D reconstruction difficult.
Capturing diverse and realistic interactions in natural settings is challenging and expensive.
Many datasets are limited in scale or diversity, restricting the generalization of learned models.
Modeling the complex dynamics of full-body interactions with articulated objects is computationally intensive.

families.name: Simulation and Benchmarking
families.definition: Platforms and datasets that provide realistic environments, objects, and tasks for training and evaluating embodied AI and robotics.

properties.text: These simulators support physics-based interaction with articulated objects, including rigid and deformable bodies.
They provide large-scale datasets with rich annotations for parts, kinematics, and semantics.
Benchmarks define specific tasks like navigation, manipulation, and human-robot collaboration.
Some platforms enable human-in-the-loop interaction via VR or other interfaces.
They aim to bridge the gap between synthetic training data and real-world applications.

limitations.text: Creating high-fidelity, large-scale datasets of articulated objects is expensive and time-consuming.
Simulations may not perfectly capture the complexities of real-world physics and sensing.
Generalization from synthetic to real-world environments remains a key challenge.
Many simulators lack the diversity of object categories and interaction types found in real homes.
Scarcity of large-scale, high-quality 3D articulated object data with detailed annotations remains a major obstacle.
Generalizing manipulation and perception models to unseen object categories and novel instances is difficult.
Achieving physically plausible and high-fidelity generation of articulated objects is challenging.
Real-time reconstruction and manipulation of articulated objects in dynamic, unstructured environments is an open problem.
Bridging the sim-to-real gap for robot manipulation of articulated objects requires better transferability.
Understanding and modeling complex, full-body human-object interactions with articulated objects is under-explored.
Inferring complete kinematic hierarchies and part connectivity for arbitrary objects without prior templates is unsolved.
